case_name: CASE OF SIC - SOCIEDADE INDEPENDENTE DE COMUNICAÇÃO, S.A v. PORTUGAL (No. 2)

assessment.1. Interference with Article 10: The Supreme Court’s judgment ordering the applicant broadcaster to pay EUR 40,000 in damages, delete the recordings from its website, and seek removal of the same material from YouTube amounted to a clear interference with its freedom to impart information and audiovisual content (see paragraph 17). The case concerns editorial choices in a documentary series and a promotional trailer about a comedian’s career, so Article 10 is engaged even though the speech was not political but largely artistic and entertainment-based.

assessment.2. Lawfulness and legitimate aim: The interference appears to have been prescribed by law, being based on Articles 70, 79, 483 and related provisions of the Civil Code, read together with the definition of consent in the Personal Data Protection Law (see paragraphs 21-22). Those provisions were accessible and, for a professional broadcaster, sufficiently foreseeable in their core effect: broadcasting identifiable images and voices of private persons without valid consent may trigger civil liability. The measure also pursued a legitimate aim, namely the protection of the rights of others, in particular the claimants’ image, reputation and dignity (see paragraphs 17-18, 20-22).

assessment.3. Applicable balancing criteria and con: The decisive issue is necessity and proportionality. In cases involving Article 10 and personality rights, the Court usually examines whether domestic courts balanced the competing interests using criteria such as contribution to a debate of public interest, notoriety of the persons concerned, their prior conduct, the circumstances in which the material was obtained, and the content, form and consequences of publication (see nos. 39954/08, 40660/08, 60641/08, 40454/07). Here, the persons shown were ordinary members of the audience, not public figures (see paragraphs 3 and 14). That weighs in favour of protection of their image. However, the exchange occurred in a theatre during a live stand-up performance, after a visible notice that the show was being recorded and after the comedian had announced that fact; cameras were openly filming both stage and audience (see paragraphs 4 and 7). The applicants then voluntarily intervened in a public and heated exchange audible to the entire auditorium (see paragraph 7). Their expectation of privacy was therefore reduced.

assessment.4. Deficiencies in the domestic proporti: The strongest point in favour of a violation is that the Supreme Court treated the case largely as one of consent and image rights, stating that the comedian’s freedom of expression was not at issue, instead of carrying out an express and careful balancing of the broadcaster’s Article 10 rights against the claimants’ interests (see paragraph 18). Yet domestic law itself contemplated exceptions where consent was not required for images captured in a public place or in connection with an event taking place in public or a matter of public interest (see paragraph 21, Article 79 § 2). The relevant Strasbourg question was not simply whether there was express consent, but whether use of the footage in the documentary and trailer was proportionate having regard to all the circumstances. The Supreme Court did consider that the footage had been edited, used out of context and made to appear ridiculing (see paragraph 18), which were relevant factors. Still, it did not adequately examine other factors that favoured the broadcaster: the open recording conditions, the applicants’ voluntary intervention, the documentary context, and the cultural or public-interest dimension of showing audience reaction to a comedian whose material itself touched on racism and offensive humour (see paragraphs 5-11 and 18).

assessment.5. Severity of the sanctions and overall: The sanctions were also significant: repeated civil liability despite the broadcaster’s reliance on contractual assurances from the producer (see paragraph 8), EUR 15,000 in moral damages plus EUR 25,000 expressly framed as punitive and deterrent damages, and a broad deletion/removal order extending to third-party platforms (see paragraph 17). Such measures were capable of producing a chilling effect, especially in documentary and broadcast contexts. While the repeated broadcasts, online availability and close-up use of the claimants’ images clearly strengthened the privacy side of the balance (see paragraphs 9-13), the domestic reasoning did not sufficiently show why those interests required so weighty a sanction instead of a narrower remedy. Given the reduced expectation of privacy in the specific setting and the insufficient Article 10 balancing by the Supreme Court, the interference is likely to be considered disproportionate under the standards reflected in nos. 39954/08, 40660/08, 60641/08, 40454/07 and 56925/08.
